summary: Argues that systems sharing resources over the ARPANET should use mechanisms designed for computer-to-computer communication, rather than opening Telnet connections and typing command strings as a person would. It sketches an approach to system interconnection.

eli5.summary: Computers were pretending to be people typing at each other. The author says machines should talk in a way built for machines.

questions: why not use telnet between programs
why computer protocols instead of telnet simulation
subtitle: Designing computers to work together as modular network services rather than pretending to be users.

tldr.problem: Early ARPANET resource sharing relied on computers emulating human users typing commands. This did not scale and ignored how computers actually work.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes that network systems should be designed from the start as composable services with defined protocols and interfaces, allowing other systems to call them directly instead of simulating user interaction.
tldr.outcome: This vision influenced the development of service-oriented architecture and laid groundwork for future network protocol design, though the full realization took decades.

today: RFC 592 is an influential early statement of what later became service-oriented architecture and microservices design. The principles it describes remain central to modern network system design.

sections.title: The Problem with Emulation
sections.content:
Early ARPANET resource sharing relied on a workaround: one computer would open a Telnet connection to another and send command strings as if a person were typing. This worked for experimentation but was inefficient and did not match how computers actually operate.

Watson argues that systems should instead be designed with computer-to-computer communication protocols from the beginning, allowing direct access to services rather than simulating user interaction.
sections.eli5: Old way: one computer pretended to be a person typing to another computer. New way: computers should talk in their own language.

sections.title: Service Modules and Composition
sections.content:
The RFC sketches a vision where every system on the network exposes a set of service modules—well-defined, reusable building blocks with documented interfaces and network connection procedures. Any system builder could then combine these services to build new systems, integrating them into their own user interface.

The RFC uses the NLS Journal as an example: its features (distribution, recording, cataloging, retrieval) could be decoupled and offered as separate services that other systems could call directly over the network.
sections.eli5: Instead of one big system doing everything, break it into pieces (like shipping, storing, and finding mail) so any computer can use just the pieces it needs.

sections.title: Challenges Ahead
sections.content:
Watson lists seven challenges to making this vision real: defining network connection types, handling structured data translation, managing responsiveness across distances, documenting interfaces, designing accounting systems, handling errors across machine boundaries, and defining standard parameter formats.

The RFC concludes that while these ideas are not new, they require a shift in how system designers think and real, working examples to become normal practice.
sections.eli5: Making it work is hard: systems need to agree on how to talk, how to pass complex data, and who pays for what.
